details: Reactor period T_r: characteristic time for power to change by factor e (~2.718); exact equation (prompt-jump approximation): T_r ≈ Λ/(ρ - β_eff) for ρ < β_eff (subcritical on prompt; delayed-neutron controlled); where: Λ = prompt neutron lifetime (s); ρ = reactivity ($); β_eff = delayed neutron fraction = 0.0065 for U-235; for RBMK at design conditions: Λ = 0.001-0.002 s (graphite moderator; longer than LWR); β_eff = 0.0065; at ρ = +0.003 (below prompt critical): T_r = 0.002 / (0.003 - 0.0065) = 0.002 / (-0.0035) = NEGATIVE → power FALLING; at ρ = +0.007 (above β_eff = prompt critical): T_r = 0.002 / (0.007 - 0.0065) = 0.002 / 0.0005 = 4 seconds (FAST RISING)
accident_application: Chernobyl accident reactivity sequence: ORM=8 (insufficient negative reactivity margin); xenon pit present (~15 β equivalent negative reactivity); at AZ-5 insertion 01:23:40: positive graphite tip effect +2-3β; already subcooled coolant flash-boiling +4-8β void; total positive reactivity +7-10β = WELL above β_eff=0.0065; ρ >> β_eff → PROMPT CRITICAL; reactor period: T_r = 0.002 / (0.007 - 0.0065) = 4 seconds... but actual ρ was +7-10β = +0.045-0.065; T_r = 0.002 / (0.065 - 0.0065) = 0.002 / 0.0585 = 34 MILLISECONDS; power doubling time ~ 24ms; from 200 MWth to 30,000 MWth in ~4 seconds = exp(4/0.034) ≈ confirming +150× power in few seconds

details: Delayed neutron groups for U-235 fission: 6 groups by precursor half-life: Group 1: t½=55.6s; β_i=0.000215 (3.3% of total β_eff); precursor: Br-87; Group 2: t½=22.1s; β_i=0.001424 (21.9%); precursor: Br-88; Group 3: t½=6.00s; β_i=0.001274 (19.6%); precursors: Rb-89; I-137; Group 4: t½=2.23s; β_i=0.002568 (39.5%); precursors: I-138; Br-89; Group 5: t½=0.496s; β_i=0.000748 (11.5%); Group 6: t½=0.179s; β_i=0.000273 (4.2%); total β_eff = 0.0065 (0.65%); 99.35% of neutrons are prompt; 0.65% delayed; mean delayed neutron lifetime = Σ(β_i × t½_i) / β_eff ≈ 13 seconds (groups 1-6 weighted average)
accident_application: Significance of 13s mean delayed lifetime: this is WHY reactors are controllable by delayed neutrons; prompt neutrons alone (Λ=0.001s) → control rod insertion must occur in milliseconds (impossible); delayed neutrons (mean 13s) → effectively Λ_eff = Λ + β_eff×<l_d> ≈ 0.001 + 0.0065×13 = 0.085 s; control rod response (~0.5-1s) is FASTER than 0.085s effective generation time → reactor is controllable; ONLY AS LONG AS ρ < β_eff; once ρ > β_eff (prompt critical): Λ reverts to 0.001s → uncontrollable by mechanical rods; Chernobyl: ρ >> β_eff → rods useless once excursion started; rods moving at 0.4 m/s × 18s = 7.2m travel needed = 18 seconds to full insertion; excursion complete in 4 seconds
source: rbmk_core_neutron_physics_REAL.csv; Lamarsh 2001 Nuclear Reactor Theory; Glasstone Sesonske 1967

details: Reactivity in dollar ($) units: 1 $ = β_eff = prompt critical boundary; <1 $: reactor subcritical on prompt neutrons; controllable by delayed neutrons; >1 $: prompt critical; exponential power rise on prompt generation time; 1 $ = 0.0065 for U-235; historical use: coined by Louis Slotin (Manhattan Project; same Slotin who died in 1946 criticality accident); 0.01 $ = 1 cent = 0.000065; cents used for small reactivity changes; practical reactor: operating at ~0.3-0.7 $/day worth of reactivity change by control rods during normal operation; xenon poisoning: up to -15 $ reactivity; void coefficient RBMK: +4-8% Δk/k per % void = +0.6-1.2 $/% void; RBMK at 200 MWth: voids forming → rapid + reactivity addition per second
accident_application: Chernobyl reactivity quantification: initial ORM=8 rods: estimated -4.5 $ residual shutdown margin (vs required -15 $ = 30 rods); at 01:23:40 AZ-5 press: (1) graphite tips inserted simultaneously → +2-3 $ instantaneous positive reactivity; (2) coolant flash boiling: void formation at 200 MWth → 80% void fraction possible rapidly → +7 $ from void coefficient; (3) total positive reactivity: +7-10 $ ≈ +$8 typical estimate; in 0.034s doubling time domain: power doubles 118 times in 4 seconds = theoretical ×10^35 → limited by fuel vaporization energy; actual: from 200 MWth → fuel energy deposition of ~300 GJ (Akimov estimates)

details: Four-factor formula k_∞ = η × ε × p × f (infinite medium): η = neutrons produced per absorption in fuel = ν × σ_f / (σ_f + σ_c) = 2.065 for U-235; 2.091 for Pu-239; ε = fast fission factor = 1.03-1.05 (fast fissions in U-238); p = resonance escape probability = 0.75-0.85 (depends on U-238 resonance integral and moderator slowing power); f = thermal utilization = σ_a_fuel / σ_a_total = 0.70-0.85 (fraction of thermal neutrons absorbed by fuel vs. by moderator + structure + coolant); k_∞ ≈ 2.065 × 1.04 × 0.80 × 0.75 = 1.29 (typical fresh LWR value > 1 = excess for control rod absorption); multiplication factor: k_eff = k_∞ × P_NL where P_NL = non-leakage probability (finite core effect)
accident_application: RBMK four-factor specifics: moderator = graphite (good moderator; C scatter cross section 4.75 barns; absorption 0.0035 barns; ξ = 0.158 mean lethargy gain per collision; need ~100 collisions to thermalize vs 18 for H₂O); f is different: graphite absorbs very little → f higher than LWR; p affected by heterogeneous geometry (fuel channels in graphite); coolant (H₂O) absorbs thermal neutrons (σ_a ~0.332 barns for H); removing H₂O → increases f (less absorption) → k_eff increases; THIS IS VOID COEFFICIENT PHYSICS → Removing H₂O coolant increases k_eff because H₂O is absorber; graphite remains as moderator; net k_eff increase = positive void coefficient
source: Lamarsh 2001; Glasstone Sesonske 1967; Duderstadt Hamilton 1976; rbmk_core_neutron_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_void_coefficient_physics_REAL.csv

details: Nuclear chain reaction: single thermal neutron fission in U-235: average ν = 2.436 neutrons produced per fission; ε = fast fission in U-238 → ~2.5 neutrons total; p = ~80% escape resonance capture; f = ~80% absorbed by fuel; η = of those in fuel, 85% cause fission; after one generation: k_∞ = ν×ε×p×f×η_correction = 1.0 (at critical); subcritical: k_eff < 1 → chain reaction dies; critical: k_eff = 1 → sustained power; supercritical: k_eff > 1 → growing power; prompt critical: k_eff > 1 + β_eff = 1.0065 → growing on prompt neutrons alone; number of generations from 200 MWth to 30,000 MWth: n = log(30,000/200) / log(k_eff) = log(150) / log(1.1) = 2.176 / 0.0414 = 52.6 generations; at Λ=0.002s: 52.6 × 0.002s = 0.105s for 150× power rise if k_eff=1.1; matches observed 4-second rise with some flux redistribution effects
accident_application: From atomic number to accident: U-235 nucleus (92 protons; 143 neutrons); neutron capture → compound nucleus U-236 → fission → ~150 amu + ~84 amu fragments + 2-3 neutrons + ~200 MeV; nuclear shell model: N=50 and N=82 stability → bimodal fission → Sr-90 (N=50) and Cs-137 (N=82) dominant; Xe-135 (N=81; near shell closure) → giant resonance cross-section 2.65×10⁶ barns; this chain from QCD → magic numbers → fission yield → Xe-135 resonance → xenon pit → ORM violation → accident; entire quantum mechanical foundation determines 1986 accident sequence

details: SCRAM (emergency shutdown) rod insertion dynamics: AZ-5 (emergency button; pressed 01:23:40): initiates simultaneous full insertion of all 187 SCRAM rods (from 211 total minus ~24 already inserted); rod insertion drive: hydraulic; insertion speed: 0.4 m/s; full insertion time: 12 m core height / 0.4 m/s = 30 seconds (original RBMK); modified post-1986: increased speed → 12 seconds; problem April 26: graphite tip effect; rod geometry: 6.7m absorber + 4.5m graphite tip; when partially inserted (1-5m): graphite tip enters positive-reactivity region at core bottom → +1.5-2 $/second momentary positive reactivity spike before absorber portion reaches positive region; this is the 'graphite tip effect' = worst case for partially-inserted rods
accident_application: AZ-5 press → INCREASED power: because partially inserted rods (1-5m deep) had graphite tips in the lower core region → inserting tips ADDED positive reactivity before absorber section reached; this effect was NOT DOCUMENTED in operator training materials; first published analysis: INSAG-1 1986 (attributed to operator error only); INSAG-7 1992: explicitly identified graphite tip as design fault; post-modification: graphite tips shortened from 4.5m to 1.25m → tip effect from +2-3 $ to <0.5 $; combined with higher ORM (30 rods minimum): modified RBMK cannot have 1986-type accident; see rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv for full modification list

details: Historical criticality accidents context: Slotin 1946 Los_Alamos: Louis Slotin manually lowered beryllium hemisphere over Pu-239 core (dragon's tail experiment); screwdriver slipped; reflected criticality excursion; 1000 rad to Slotin in 0.25s; Slotin died 9 days later (ARS); assembly promptly separated by hand; accident terminated; Daghlian 1945: same core; neutron reflector error; died 25 days post-exposure; SL-1 1961 Idaho: naval reactor; manually withdrawn control rod 41cm; prompt criticality; steam explosion; 3 deaths; one worker pinned to ceiling by control rod; IAEA lists 60 criticality accidents globally 1945-2010; Tokaimura 1999 (Japan): Pu solution over-concentration; 2 deaths; population evacuated; all involved uncontrolled criticality
accident_application: "Chernobyl vs. historical criticality accidents: Chernobyl was an in-pile criticality in a running 3200 MWth power reactor; scale incomparable to laboratory/processing criticalities; energy released ~300 GJ vs ~0.003 GJ (Tokaimura); Chernobyl prompt critical excursion lasted ~4 seconds → entire reactor destroyed; historical criticality accidents = much smaller but same physics; all criticality accidents contribute to: (1) operator training databases; (2) IAEA criticality safety standards; (3) fissile material handling protocols; criticality safety = preventing k_eff from reaching 1.0; geometrical control; concentration limits; neutron absorbers; moderation limitation"
source: Lamarsh 2001; McLaughlin 2000 A Review of Criticality Accidents LA-13638; IAEA-TECDOC-1706; nuclear_accident_history_comparison_REAL.csv

details: Subcritical multiplication factor M: M = 1/(1-k); for subcritical assembly (k < 1): even with external neutron source S, steady-state neutron population = M × (neutrons from source × generation time); as k → 1 (approaching critical): M → ∞; measurement: subcritical approach plot (1/M vs control rod position); when 1/M → 0 = predicted critical point; safety rule: do not approach closer than predicted critical without pause; significance for CORIUM (Room 305/2 at Chernobyl): fissile material in corium; water infiltration = moderator → could increase k; neutron flux DOUBLED 2016-2021 as water percolated through corium; SNRIU and SSE CHNPP monitoring: confirmed subcritical (k << 1) but watching; drainage improvements after NSC: reduced water → flux stabilized 2022
accident_application: Room 305/2 subcriticality confidence: current corium geometry + composition: k_eff estimated ~0.5-0.7 (well subcritical) but: (1) composition uncertain (corium composition surveys 2016-2021 showed heterogeneous FCM); (2) water geometry uncertain; (3) neutron source = Am-241 alpha → (α,n) reactions in light elements; safety argument: corium criticality accident requires: sufficient fissile mass (present, ~100 kg Pu); adequate moderation (water infiltration = concern); adequate geometry (current random geometry highly unfavorable); IAEA assessment: no criticality risk under current conditions; NSC drainage goal: reduce moisture → increase subcriticality margin
